subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Electronic Stability Control
description: A short lesson to help you apply Electronic Stability Control.

hook.text: In 1997, a Mercedes A-Class flipped during a Swedish magazine test called the Moose Test.

buildup.text: The embarrassing video went viral and threatened to destroy the new model's reputation.

discovery.text: Mercedes rushed out electronic stability control—software that brakes individual wheels to stop skids.

twist.text: What began as a PR crisis became the most important safety feature since the seatbelt.

climax.text: ESC prevents roughly one-third of all fatal crashes and two-thirds of all rollovers.

punchline.text: A failed magazine test launched a lifesaving technology.

quiz.question: What event accelerated adoption of electronic stability control?
options: The Mercedes A-Class Moose Test failure

details.summary: Electronic stability control detects when a car begins to skid and automatically applies individual brakes to specific wheels, helping the driver maintain control during emergency maneuvers.
details.whyItMatters: ESC reduces single-vehicle crashes by up to 40 percent and has been mandatory on new cars in the US and EU since the early 2010s, preventing countless rollovers and spinouts.
takeaways: ESC compares steering input to actual vehicle direction
It brakes individual wheels to correct skids instantly
Mandated in many countries since the early 2010s

faq.question: Is electronic stability control the same as traction control?
faq.answer: They are related but different. Traction control prevents wheel spin during acceleration, while ESC intervenes during cornering or emergency swerves to prevent the whole car from skidding.

faq.question: Can ESC be turned off, and should drivers ever do so?
faq.answer: Most cars allow ESC to be partially or fully disabled. This is useful only in specific situations like driving in deep sand or snow where wheel spin is needed to gain traction.
